In this sequence of operations, it is assumed that a teleoperations session has already been established between the autonomous vehicle and the teleoperations system, e.g., based upon a condition sensed by the autonomous vehicle, based upon monitoring by a teleoperations system operator, based upon a scheduled teleoperations session, etc. It may also be assumed that at this time context data, e.g., autonomy, sensor, telemetry and/or video data, is being streamed from the autonomous vehicle to the teleoperations system, and is being presented by the teleoperations system to the teleoperations system operator, e.g., via a graphical user interface, as described above in connection with FIG. 4.

Assume in block 522, operator virtual path sug-gestion input is received from a teleoperations system opera-tor to define a virtual path of travel (e.g., by touching or clicking control 370 of FIG. 6). As illustrated in FIG. 14, for example, operator input to define a virtual path of travel may be based upon an operator touching or clicking on a plurality of points 396, to which a curve may be fit to define a virtual path of travel, and which may be displayed to an operator as illustrated at 398. It will be appreciated that an innumerable number of types of interactions may be used to receive operator input and display a virtual path of travel, so the invention is not limited to this particular interaction. It will be appreciated, for example, that an operator may be per-mitted to trace the path by dragging along a desired course. An operator may also be able to edit the path, e.g., by moving one or more points 396, adding additional points, deleting points, etc. In addition, in some instances points 396 may be created prior to selecting control 370, whereby control 370 effectively generates the path data based upon the currently-displayed points.

Returning to FIG. 13, upon receipt of the operator virtual path suggestion input, the teleoperations system may locally validate the input, and block 524 may determine if the input was validated, and if not, pass control to block 526 to reject the input and notify the operator. For example, if the virtual path is determined to cross a hard road boundary, or any other constraint described above, the virtual path suggestion input may be rejected.

Returning to block 524, if the input passes the initial validation, control passes to block 528 to optionally perform one or more operations to utilize this operator input more broadly by the overall system. For example, in some implementations, the event data associated with the virtual path suggestion may be stored as training data, e.g., to assist in training and improving the performance of a machine learning model used by an autonomous vehicle. As one example, the context data associated with the virtual path suggestion, as well as the fact that the virtual path suggestion input was entered by an operator, may be used to reinforce a perception component's assessment that what was perceived in front of the vehicle was related to construction, thereby improving the detection of construction by the perception component.

In addition, in some implementations, block 524 may propagate path data for the virtual path of travel to other vehicles in a fleet of vehicles. By doing so, other vehicles may potentially implement the same path when such vehicles approach the same geographic location. Further, in some implementations, block 524 may schedule a teleop-erations session for another vehicle to reassess the event at a later point in time.

Next, block 530 generates path data corresponding to the virtual path suggestion input and communicates the path data to the vehicle, which is received in block 532. In some implementations, the path data may include multiple points on a map or another definition of a path, e.g., one or more line and/or curved segments.

Block 534 next validates the path data from the perspective of the autonomous vehicle. Validation, for example, may determine whether the virtual path defined by the path data violates any perception or other vehicle con-straints, as well as any hard road boundaries. As noted above, however, validation may be different from validation performed in other scenarios, e.g., to validate virtual paths that would ordinary not be validated in the absence of performing a virtual path suggestion operation. Thus, for example, validation may occur even in the presence of traffic controls, lane boundaries and/or directions of travel that otherwise would be violated during ordinary operation of the autonomous vehicle.

If the path data fails validation, block 536 passes control to block 538 to reject the path data and notify the teleoperations system. Otherwise, block 536 passes control to block 540 to generate and execute a path based upon the path data, and upon completion of the execution, passes control to block 542 to wait for further operator input. In particular, in the illustrated implementation, virtual path suggestion may be limited to situations where the vehicle is already stopped, and as illustrated in block 544, the genera-tion and execution of the path in block 540 may be per-formed in three phases. In a first phase, a vehicle hold is released and in a second phase, the vehicle traverses the virtual path, generally at a lower maximum speed (which may be determined, e.g., based upon other lanes in the vicinity or based on hard coding for virtual path suggestion). It will be appreciated that during this traversal, the vehicle will continue to validate the initially validated path to maintain adherence to current vehicle and environmental constraints. Then, in a third phase, a stop and hold may be performed to bring the vehicle to a stop at the end of the virtual path and provide an ability for the teleoperations system operator to assess the current context and either provide another virtual path suggestion input or utilize other teleoperations functionality. Also, in some implementations, at the end of a virtual path, the autonomous vehicle may resume normal operation, and automatically reroute based upon original mapping data. In some instances, however, resumption of normal operation may be deferred until a hold is released.

Virtual Path Suggestion Constraints

In some implementations, it may also be desirable to incorporate constraints on virtual path suggestions to assist in guiding a teleoperations system operator during generation of virtual path suggestions. In particular, as noted above, virtual path suggestions may be used in situations where a relatively complex path is needed to traverse through a drivable space that is not mapped with autono-mous lanes, and where lane closures or openings are insuf-ficient to enable an autonomous vehicle to determine a suitable path for addressing a particular condition. In these situations, defining a virtual path of travel through a com-plex region may be further complicated by the fact that an autonomous vehicle may have various physical attributes that constrain or limit the movement of the autonomous vehicle.

One such physical attribute for some autonomous vehicles is a minimum turning radius, which relates to the tightest turn that the autonomous vehicle can make based upon the range of travel of the steering components of the autonomous vehicle. The minimum turning radius is gener-ally a mechanical limitation of the autonomous vehicle, and in many cases is independent of the velocity of the autono-mous vehicle. In some implementations, for example, mini-mum turning radius may be calculated as (wheelbase/tan

(max road wheel angle)), although other calculations may be used in other implementations.

Another such physical attribute for some autono-mous vehicles is trailer sweep or off-tracking. In particular, for autonomous vehicles that pull a trailer, such as tractor trailers, the tracks of the rear wheels of the trailer will generally diverge from the tracks of the wheels of the autonomous vehicle, particularly when turning, such that the maximum swept path of the autonomous vehicle and its trailer when traversing along a virtual path of travel is effectively wider than the physical width of the autonomous vehicle and trailer when driving in a straight line. When making turns at intersections, for example, truck drivers are taught to "square off" the turns by pulling the truck forward some distance into an intersection before beginning the turn to ensure that the wheels of the trailer are sufficiently in the intersection so that they will not cut across the corner.

As such, in some implementations, it may be desirable to incorporate constraints on virtual path sugges-tions to assist in guiding a teleoperations system operator during generation of virtual path suggestions, e.g., while receiving virtual path suggestion inputs from a teleopera-tions system operator. A virtual path suggestion constraint, in this regard, may be considered to be a constraint placed on how a virtual path suggestion may be generated, and that is based in part on a physical attribute of the autonomous vehicle that limits, in some fashion, the movement of the autonomous vehicle. This is in contrast to environmental constraints, such as due to static objects, dynamic objects or actors, boundaries, etc. that are present in the environment but are separate from the autonomous vehicle.

In some implementations, virtual path suggestion constraints may be used to guide a teleoperations system operator during generation of a virtual path suggestion, e.g., through the display or presentation of one or more visual guides on a teleoperations user interface prior to and/or during generation of a virtual path suggestion (e.g., while defining a virtual path of travel). A visual guide, for example, may be overlaid on a two or three dimensional map representation of the environment surrounding the autono-mous vehicle, and may be used to define areas or volumes of the map where a virtual path of travel defined by a virtual path suggestion is not permitted to enter or intersect, e.g., due to its minimum turning radius and/or due to any trailer sweep associated with a portion of the virtual path of travel.

In some implementations, virtual path suggestion constraints may also be presented in conjunction with vari-ous environmental constraints. For example, it may be desirable in some implementations to present ground slope. In particular, while some shoulders are relatively flat, others may have a slope that may be excessively steep for navi-gation of the autonomous vehicle. Thus, by presenting ground slope information, e.g., by shading areas of the shoulder or overlaying a virtual boundary on the shoulder, a teleoperations system operator may be guided to avoid generating a virtual path suggestion that would navigate the autonomous vehicle onto an excessively steep shoulder.

In addition, in some implementations, virtual path suggestion constraints may be used to validate a virtual path suggestion, such that a teleoperations system operator may be notified that a violation of a virtual path suggestion constraint has occurred and that the virtual path of travel defined by a virtual path suggestion cannot be accepted. Further, in some implementations, the notifications may be used to identify a location in the environment where a violation has occurred, e.g., through highlighting a portion of a teleoperations user interface, such as within a map, such that a teleoperations system operator can readily identify where a violation has occurred and potentially how to modify the virtual path of travel to avoid any violations.

Virtual path suggestion constraints may be deter-mined in a number of manners in different implementations. For example, virtual path suggestion constraints may be statically defined in some implementations and/or hard coded into logic, while in other implementations, virtual path suggestion constraints may be dynamically determined, e.g., based on the current pose of the autonomous vehicle, the current motion (velocity, acceleration, direction, etc.) of the autonomous vehicle, the virtual path of travel (or portion of the virtual path of travel) being generated, etc. A virtual path suggestion constraint may also be specific to a particu-lar type or model of autonomous vehicle and/or may be based at least in part on one or more physical characteristics of the autonomous vehicle, e.g., dimensions, wheelbase, number of wheels and/or axles, weight, and various mechanical constraints such as range of motion of steering components, etc. Such characteristics may be stored in a teleoperations system in some implementations, or may be supplied to a teleoperations system by an autonomous vehicle in some implementations.
